title: Phones Handed In in the Morning: Different Voices
in_one_line: A father wants his daughter’s school to collect phones all day, while a nurse and a working student worry about what that could interrupt. They disagree about when phones should be handed in, but all want to stay able to talk to someone.
part1: I want my daughter's high school to hold onto the phones. Collect them all in the morning. Give them back when school lets out. Until then, they stay handed in. Then I wouldn't be the only bad guy. We agreed that at night, she'd put her phone in a basket in the living room. My daughter didn't keep that promise. I took her phone away. The next morning, breakfast was quiet. All I could hear was the sound of dishes. I wanted her to stick to what we'd agreed, but after I took her phone, I was the one who couldn't look her in the face. I don't want another morning like that. It would help if I could say the school was doing the same thing. I'm tired of arguing every night. But I just want to push this onto the school. At work, I'm the one who makes the arrangements. At home, I want to get out of being the bad guy. I'm a dad asking the school to come to my rescue.
part2: “I'm sleepy,” they say. Every morning, I see the faces of kids who come to the nurse's office first thing, and I wonder what else is behind that word. The other day, a phone screen was glowing beside the pillow of a child resting on a bed. I couldn't look away from that glow. I wanted to ask about last night, but what would happen if they thought I was a teacher who takes phones away? Would they still talk to me? If we collect all the phones in the morning and don't give them back until school lets out, can we say that's enough? I'm afraid that once we've collected the phones, we'll think everything is fine. I want that child to be able to talk about what happens at night. I don't want the nurse's office to be a place where phones are taken away. After we take a phone in, who will listen to that child?
part3: I sort packages in a warehouse during the day, and go to evening high school at night. But I can't hand in my phone until school lets out. I can keep my promise not to touch it during class. During breaks, I want to answer work messages. Before, calls from work kept coming during class. I couldn't answer, and the missed calls just kept piling up on my screen. Later, they told me it was a problem that they couldn't reach me. I almost had my shifts cut. I give the money I earn to my family. I want to earn my workplace's trust myself. But I don't want to quit school. I've started to understand the lessons here. I don't want to choose between work and school. I promise I'll keep my phone at the bottom of my bag during class. So please listen to what I have to say before deciding.
part4: At the breakfast table, beside the pillow in the nurse's office, and when work messages come, people want to stay able to talk to the other person. The school's phone collection might reduce arguments over the basket at night, but it could cut off a conversation by the pillow. It might protect learning in class, but if it also stops messages about shifts during breaks, trust at work could be shaken. The father asking the school for help also doesn't want to go through the silence after taking the phone away again. They may disagree about how long phones should be handed in, but they share a wish to still have someone they can talk to. What message do you want to answer right away? When does it come, and who sends it?
